# Partition Suit in Rajasthan: Family Property Division Procedure
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/partition-suit-family-property-rajasthan.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Partition Suits in Rajasthan: How Family Property Is Divided Under Law

Property Law

# Partition Suits in Rajasthan: How Family Property Is Divided Under Law

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 June 2026

Few disputes are as common — or as emotionally charged — in Rajasthan as the division of family property. Whether it is an ancestral haveli in the old city, agricultural khasras in the village, or a jointly purchased commercial plot, the legal route to converting an undivided share into separately owned property is the partition suit. Understanding how partition actually works — who can claim, in which court, at what cost, and over what timeline — prevents both unrealistic expectations and avoidable litigation.

Two different things called "partition": In Hindu law, partition has a dual meaning. First, the severance of joint status — the moment a coparcener unequivocally communicates an intention to separate, the joint family status is severed in law and shares crystallise, even before any physical division. Second, the partition by metes and bounds — the actual physical division of properties into separately possessed and owned parcels. A suit for partition seeks both: a declaration of the plaintiff's share, and its physical separation.

Daughters are equal coparceners — Vineeta Sharma: Since the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a daughter is a coparcener in her father's ancestral (coparcenary) property by birth, with rights equal to a son. The Supreme Court's three-judge bench in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) settled the controversy conclusively: the daughter's coparcenary right arises by birth and does not depend on the father being alive on the date of the amendment. In practical terms, a married daughter in Rajasthan today has the same right to demand partition of ancestral property as her brothers, and to seek her share of agricultural land in the revenue records.

Civil court or revenue court — choosing the right forum: This is the single most common jurisdictional trap in Rajasthan property litigation. Partition of agricultural land held in khatedari tenure is governed by Section 53 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and falls within the jurisdiction of the revenue courts (the Sub-Divisional Officer at first instance, with appeals up the revenue hierarchy to the Board of Revenue) — a civil court's decree partitioning khatedari land is open to serious jurisdictional objection. Partition of houses, urban plots, and other non-agricultural property goes to the civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Where a single family corpus includes both kinds of property, parallel proceedings are often unavoidable, and they must be strategically coordinated so that admissions in one do not damage the other.

How a civil partition suit proceeds: The suit is filed by any co-owner against all other co-owners (every co-owner must be a party — a partition decree binds the entire body of co-sharers). The court first determines the shares and passes a preliminary decree declaring them. It then moves to the working-out stage under Order XX Rule 18 CPC: for revenue-paying estates the partition may be referred to the Collector; for other immovable property the court ordinarily appoints a Local Commissioner to propose a division by metes and bounds, adjusting inequalities through owelty (equalisation payments). Where a property is incapable of fair physical division — a single shop, a small dwelling — the court can direct sale and distribution of proceeds, and a co-sharer may invoke the Partition Act, 1893 to buy out the share of another at valuation. The final decree then records the division, and it is this decree that is executed and mutated.

Common defences and complications: (1) Prior partition — the defendants assert that an oral partition already occurred decades ago; the court examines conduct, separate possession, separate revenue entries and tax records. (2) Family settlement — a fair and bona fide family arrangement, even oral, is binding under the principles of Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation (1976); a memorandum that merely records a past settlement does not require registration. (3) Self-acquired versus ancestral character — only coparcenary property is partible as of right; self-acquired property of a living owner is not. (4) Ouster and limitation — possession of one co-owner is ordinarily possession of all; a co-owner pleading adverse possession against their own family must prove open and hostile ouster for the statutory period, a deliberately difficult standard. (5) Alienations — sales by one co-sharer of specific portions bind only that sharer's undivided interest, and the purchaser steps into an undivided share, subject to equities at the time of final division.

Court fees and timeline in Rajasthan: Under the Rajasthan Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1961, a plaintiff who is in joint possession of the property pays only a fixed court fee; a plaintiff who has been excluded from possession must pay ad valorem fee on the value of their share — a difference that can run into lakhs and that shapes how the plaint is drafted. A contested partition suit through preliminary decree, commissioner proceedings and final decree typically runs several years; an uncontested or settled partition can conclude far faster. After the final decree, mutation of the divided parcels in the Jamabandi (for land) or municipal records (for urban property) completes the process.

The settlement-first approach: Because every co-sharer must eventually live with the division, mediated family settlements deserve serious consideration before — or during — litigation. A comprehensive registered partition deed, or a court decree in terms of a compromise under Order XXIII CPC, gives the family finality at a fraction of the cost of a fought-out suit. Where relations permit, a well-drafted family settlement is almost always the superior instrument; where they do not, a properly framed partition suit with interim protection (receiver, injunction against alienation, status-quo orders) safeguards the corpus while the shares are worked out.

When a co-sharer lives abroad: a partition in which one branch of the family is overseas raises questions the CPC does not answer on its own — how the absent co-sharer validly authorises an appearance, whether the twelve-year period under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 has begun to run against them, and whether a mutation already entered in the other sharers' names has to be undone before the shares can be worked out. Those are dealt with in securing inherited land in Rajasthan from abroad.

A practical note from matters of this kind at Jodhpur: where one family corpus holds a haveli in the walled city and khatedari land out in the tehsil, the two halves are heard in two different buildings. One corpus, two forums. A compromise drafted for one of them therefore has to be worded so that it concedes nothing in the other. Which court at Jodhpur receives which paper, and the chamber, hours and enrolment particulars of this office, are set out on the page for an advocate in Jodhpur.
 
This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal guidance on your matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

# Property Disputes in Rajasthan: Partition, Title, Revenue Courts
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/property-disputes-rajasthan.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Property Disputes in Rajasthan: Partition, Title and the Revenue Courts

Property Law

# Property Disputes in Rajasthan: Partition, Title and the Revenue Courts

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 April 2026

Property disputes are among the most frequently litigated matters in Rajasthan, and the first question is rarely what the dispute is about. It is which forum can hear it at all. Jurisdiction is split between the civil courts under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the revenue courts under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956, and the Board of Revenue at the apex of the revenue hierarchy. The working test is the classification of the land. A title dispute over a non-agricultural plot belongs to the civil court. Anything touching khatedari rights, mutation or land classification belongs to the revenue side. Getting this wrong is expensive, because a plaint presented in the wrong forum is returned, and by the time it is filed again the other side has usually moved the revenue record along.

A partition suit over agricultural land in Rajasthan is not a civil suit at all, and this is the point on which clients are most often misled. Section 53 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 governs the division of a holding. Entry 3 in the Part-Suits table of the Third Schedule makes a suit for division of a holding triable by the Assistant Collector, and prescribes no period of limitation for it. Section 207(1) places every suit listed in that Schedule before a revenue court, and Section 207(2) bars any other court from taking cognizance of it, or of any suit resting on a cause of action for which the revenue court could grant relief. Section 53(1) was omitted with effect from 11 November 1992. What survives is Section 53(2): a holding is divided either by agreement between the co-tenants covering both the division and the distribution of rent over the several portions, or by the decree or order of a competent court in a suit by one or more co-tenants. Section 53(4) requires every co-tenant and the landholder to be joined. Applications stall for months on that sub-section alone, because one absent co-tenant was treated as a formality.

Where a partition does belong to the civil court, Order XX Rule 18 CPC is often cited as though it were the provision under which the suit is filed. It is not. A civil suit is instituted under Section 9; Rule 18 governs the form of the decree after the court has decided to partition. The distinction decides what happens next. Under Rule 18(1), where the decree relates to an estate assessed to the payment of revenue to the Government, the court declares the rights of the several parties but must direct the partition itself to be made by the Collector, or by a gazetted subordinate deputed by him, in accordance with Section 54 CPC. A Local Commissioner has no role in that class of case. The Commissioner belongs to Rule 18(2), which covers other immovable and movable property, where the court may pass a preliminary decree declaring shares and give such further directions as are required. Where a single dwelling cannot conveniently be divided, a sale and distribution of the proceeds may be sought instead of physical division.

Title disputes arise when two parties claim ownership of the same property. The rule is that the plaintiff must prove their own title and cannot succeed on the weakness of the defendant’s (nemo dat quod non habet). Registered sale deeds, gift deeds, succession documents, mutation entries and proof of continuous possession are the ordinary material. One caution about the mutation entry: it is a fiscal record kept for the collection of revenue and does not by itself create or extinguish title, as the Rajasthan land revenue procedure sets out. Clients arrive at Jodhpur with a Jamabandi carrying their name and treat it as conclusive. It is evidence of what the revenue record says. It is not a decree of ownership.

Adverse possession is commonly described as arising under Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Section 27 does less than that. It extinguishes the owner’s right once the period limited for a suit for possession has run out, and nothing more. The period comes from the Schedule. Article 65 gives twelve years for a suit for possession of immovable property based on title, counted from the date the defendant’s possession becomes adverse to the plaintiff, which is not the date on which possession began. Against the State the figure is different. Article 112 allows thirty years for a suit by or on behalf of the Central Government or a State Government. That one difference decides a great many encroachment matters over siwai chak and other government land in this district, where twelve years is assumed and thirty is the answer. There is also no rule that a woman’s property cannot be lost to adverse possession. The actual provision is narrow: Explanation (b) to Article 65 says that where the suit is by a Hindu or Muslim entitled to possession on the death of a Hindu or Muslim female, the defendant’s possession is deemed to become adverse only when that female dies. It postpones the starting point for the reversioner. It confers no immunity.

For a buyer, due diligence in Rajasthan runs through two systems, and neither of them is a grievance portal. Revenue records, the Jamabandi and the Girdawari, are on Apna Khata at apnakhata.raj.nic.in. Registered instruments and the encumbrance position are checked through the registration department’s e-Panjiyan system and at the Sub-Registrar’s office for the tehsil in which the land falls. Pending litigation has to be searched separately on the district court and High Court portals, because nothing in a revenue record discloses an injunction. Where the seller claims through inheritance, ask for the succession document and not merely the mutation that followed it. An indemnity clause in the sale agreement is worth having, but it is a claim in damages against a person who may by then not be worth suing. The verification done before the deed is executed is worth more than the clause drafted afterwards.

Before any of this is reached the civil side settles a smaller question: which court the plaint actually goes to. Section 16 CPC fixes that by the land and not by the parties. A suit for the recovery of immovable property, for partition, for foreclosure, sale or redemption of a mortgage, or for the determination of any other right to or interest in immovable property is instituted in the court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate. The proviso is the exception worth knowing: where the relief sought can be entirely obtained through the defendant’s personal obedience, the suit may instead be brought where the defendant actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business or personally works for gain. Section 17 answers the case that recurs here, a family holding partly inside Jodhpur city and partly in a tehsil outside it. The suit may then be instituted in any court within whose limits any portion of the property is situate, but only if, in respect of the value of the subject-matter, the entire claim is cognizable by that court. Convenience does not decide it. That proviso does. Section 18 deals with the boundary that is itself uncertain: a court may record a statement of the uncertainty and proceed, and its decree stands as though the property lay within its limits, an appellate or revisional court refusing the objection later unless there was no reasonable ground for the uncertainty at institution and a failure of justice has followed. Choosing wrong is not fatal. It is slow. Order VII Rule 10 returns the plaint to be presented to the court in which the suit should have been instituted, with the date of presentation, the date of return and the reasons endorsed on it. Rule 10A is the sub-rule few plaintiffs use and most should: where the defendant has already appeared, the court must intimate its decision before returning the plaint, and on the plaintiff’s application it fixes the date of appearance before the court named for the fresh presentation and gives notice to both sides, so that no fresh summons is needed there. The price is that a plaintiff who applies under Rule 10A gives up the appeal against the order of return. Which of the forums at Jodhpur a property matter belongs to in the first place, civil or revenue, is sorted in a separate note on the courts at Jodhpur and which of them a property suit is presented to.

Frequently asked questions

Is a partition suit over agricultural land in Rajasthan filed in the civil court?
No. Section 207(1) of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 places every suit listed in the Third Schedule before a revenue court, and Entry 3 of that Schedule makes a suit for division of a holding triable by the Assistant Collector. Section 207(2) bars any other court from taking cognizance of it. A plaint for partition of khatedari land presented in the civil court at Jodhpur is returned.

Does a Jamabandi entry or a mutation prove ownership?
No. The Jamabandi is a fiscal record kept for the collection of revenue; a mutation entry records who pays, and does not by itself create or extinguish title. It is evidence of what the revenue record says. Ownership is proved through registered sale or gift deeds, succession documents and proof of possession, and the plaintiff must prove their own title rather than the weakness of the defendant's.

Which civil court hears a suit about immovable property?
Section 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 fixes it by the land: a suit for recovery of immovable property, partition, or any right to or interest in it is instituted in the court within whose local limits the property is situate. Where the property lies in two jurisdictions, for example partly in Jodhpur city and partly in a tehsil outside it, Section 17 allows the suit in either.

How long before adverse possession bars the owner's suit?
Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 gives twelve years for a suit for possession based on title, counted from the date the defendant's possession becomes adverse, not from the date it began. Against the Central or a State Government, Article 112 allows thirty years. Section 27 then extinguishes the owner's right once the period has run out; it does not itself confer title.

Who actually divides revenue-paying land after a civil partition decree?
Under Order XX Rule 18(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the decree relates to an estate assessed to the payment of revenue to the Government, the court declares the rights of the parties but the partition itself is made by the Collector, or a gazetted subordinate deputed by him, under Section 54. A Local Commissioner is appointed only under Rule 18(2), for other immovable and movable property.

This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal guidance on your matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

# SARFAESI Section 13(2) Notice: What a Borrower Can Actually Do
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/sarfaesi-section-13-2-notice-borrower-options-india.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Power of Attorney from Abroad

Banking & Recovery Law

# The bank has sent a Section 13(2) notice under the SARFAESI Act. What can a borrower actually do?

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 September 2026

Papers in hand? A photo of the notice, order or petition can be sent on WhatsApp to +91 70230 51275, or call the same number (Mon–Sat, 12 noon – 10 PM).

A notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 requires payment in full within sixty days. During that period the borrower may object in writing, and the bank must give reasons for rejecting the objection within fifteen days. The Debts Recovery Tribunal can only be approached after the bank takes possession, within forty-five days.

At a glance

Time given by the notice — sixty days from the date of the notice to discharge the liabilities in full; the account must already stand classified as a non-performing asset (Section 13(2))
 
If you object — the secured creditor must consider the representation and, if it is not accepted, communicate the reasons within fifteen days (Section 13(3A)). Those reasons do not by themselves open the door to the Tribunal (proviso to Section 13(3A); Explanation to Section 17(1))
 
What the bank may then do — take possession of the secured asset, take over the management of the business, appoint a manager, or require a debtor of the borrower to pay it directly (Section 13(4)(a) to (d))
 
Forum and limitation — an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 17(1), within forty-five days from the date the measure was taken; filed where the cause of action arises, where the secured asset is located, or where the branch keeping the account is situated (Section 17(1A))
 
How long the Tribunal has — disposal within sixty days, and total pendency not exceeding four months, extendable only for reasons recorded in writing (Section 17(5))
 
Appeal — to the Appellate Tribunal within thirty days, not entertained unless fifty per cent of the debt claimed or determined, whichever is less, is deposited; reducible for recorded reasons to not less than twenty-five per cent (Section 18)
 
Last point of redemption — the dues, with costs and charges, tendered at any time before the date of publication of the notice for public auction, quotations, tender or private treaty (Section 13(8))
 
Outside the Act altogether — a security interest created in agricultural land (Section 31(i)); a financial asset not exceeding one lakh rupees (Section 31(h)); a case where the amount due is less than twenty per cent of the principal and interest (Section 31(j))
 
Leading case — Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 8 April 2004, (2004) 4 SCC 311

Jurisdiction. The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 is a central statute and applies across India. The Debts Recovery Tribunals sit in most States, and the branch, the borrower and the mortgaged property are frequently in three different places — Section 17(1A) is what decides which Tribunal hears the matter. Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961 entitles an advocate to practise throughout India, and these matters are commonly conducted for borrowers who are not resident in the State where the security lies.

## What the sixty days are actually for

Section 13(2) is not a warning letter. It is the step that makes everything after it lawful. Two things must already be true before it can be issued: there must be a default in repayment of a secured debt, and the account must have been classified by the secured creditor as a non-performing asset. The notice must then, under Section 13(3), give the details of the amount payable and identify the secured assets the creditor intends to proceed against. If the sixty days pass without full payment, the creditor becomes entitled to take one or more of the measures in Section 13(4) — and the most consequential of them, possession of the property, needs no order of any civil court.

One restriction begins the moment the notice is received rather than when the sixty days end. Section 13(13) forbids the borrower from transferring the secured assets named in the notice by sale, lease or otherwise, except in the ordinary course of business, without the prior written consent of the secured creditor. A sale arranged in that window to raise the money — which is the first idea most borrowers have, and often a sensible one commercially — is a sale made in the teeth of the section unless the bank's written consent is taken first.

## Is there any point in replying to the notice?

There is, and it is a narrower point than most borrowers expect. Section 13(3A) was inserted after the Supreme Court in Mardia Chemicals held that where a borrower raises an objection or places facts before the secured creditor, "such reply to the notice must be considered with due application of mind and the reasons for not accepting the objections, howsoever brief they may be, must be communicated to the borrower". The section now fixes fifteen days for that communication. But the same judgment, and the proviso that Parliament enacted, are equally clear that those reasons are for the borrower's information only and give rise to no right to approach the Tribunal at that stage.

So the reply is not a remedy. It is the record. The objection that is put on paper within the sixty days — that the account was wrongly classified, that the figure demanded includes charges never debited to the account, that the property described is not the property mortgaged, that the loan is one the Act cannot reach at all — is the objection the Tribunal will later be asked to test against the bank's fifteen-day reasons. The commonest difficulty in these matters is not a bad case; it is a borrower who spent the whole sixty days negotiating at the branch counter, put nothing in writing, and arrives after possession with nothing on record but a memory of what a manager said.

## When does the right to go to the Tribunal begin?

On the day a measure under Section 13(4) is actually taken. Section 17(1) allows any person, including the borrower, aggrieved by any of those measures to apply to the Debts Recovery Tribunal within forty-five days from the date on which the measure was taken. That date is a question of fact and it is worth pinning down early, because the forty-five days run from it and not from the day the borrower learns of it, and not from the date of the bank's reasons under Section 13(3A).

What the Tribunal is asked to decide is set by Section 17(2): whether the measures taken were in accordance with the Act and the rules. If it concludes they were not, Section 17(3) empowers it to declare the recourse invalid, to restore possession or management to the borrower, and to pass such other directions as it considers necessary. This is the provision under which a property that has already gone out of the borrower's hands can come back, and it is the reason the compliance record — the notice, the objection, the reasons, the affidavit before the District Magistrate — matters more in these hearings than the story of how the business came to fail.

Section 17(5) tells the Tribunal to dispose of the application within sixty days, and caps total pendency at four months, extendable only for reasons recorded in writing. Where that is exceeded, Section 17(6) lets either party ask the Appellate Tribunal to direct expeditious disposal — a step rarely taken and worth remembering when an application has been pending far past the statutory outer limit.

## The District Magistrate's order under Section 14 — is that a hearing?

It is not, and a great deal of wasted effort follows from assuming that it is. Where the creditor needs help to take possession, Section 14 lets it apply in writing to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the District Magistrate in whose jurisdiction the asset lies, and that authority is to take possession of the asset and forward it to the creditor. The application must carry an affidavit of the authorised officer declaring nine specified things, among them that the sixty-day notice under Section 13(2) was served and that the borrower's objection was considered and reasons for non-acceptance communicated. The order is to be passed within thirty days, extendable for reasons recorded in writing but not beyond sixty days in the aggregate.

The borrower is not a party to that exercise, and Section 14(3) states that no act done by the Magistrate or the District Magistrate under the section shall be called in question in any court or before any authority. What the affidavit does give the borrower is a checklist: it is a sworn statement, filed by the bank, of the very compliances that Section 17 lets the Tribunal examine. Where one of those declarations is untrue — the notice not served, the objection never answered — the place to say so is the Tribunal, not the District Magistrate's office.

## Should a writ petition be filed in the High Court instead?

Usually not, and the reason is not a lack of jurisdiction but a rule of restraint the High Courts apply to themselves. In United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon, Supreme Court, 26 July 2010, (2010) 8 SCC 110, it was held that the High Court "will ordinarily not entertain a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution if an effective remedy is available to the aggrieved person and that this rule applies with greater rigour in matters involving recovery of taxes, cess, fees, other types of public money and the dues of banks and other financial institutions". A borrower who spends six weeks on a writ petition that is dismissed on that ground has usually also spent the forty-five days available under Section 17.

The writ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 remains what it always was for the case that genuinely falls outside the statutory scheme. But the ordinary grievance — wrong figures, defective service, possession taken without compliance — is the grievance Section 17 was written for, and it is heard by a tribunal that can restore possession, which the writ court will generally decline to do while that alternative stands unused.

## Can the property still be redeemed once the auction is announced?

Section 13(8) fixes the point at which the answer changes. If the amount due to the secured creditor, together with all costs, charges and expenses incurred by it, is tendered at any time before the date of publication of the notice for public auction, or for inviting quotations or tender from the public, or for private treaty, then the secured asset shall not be transferred, and where any step towards transfer has already been taken, no further step shall be taken. The provision was recast in 2016 and the earlier, later cut-off — the date of sale or transfer — is no longer the law. The date to work back from is therefore the publication of the sale notice, not the auction date printed on it.

That distinction decides whether a borrower who has arranged funds is in time. It is worth reading the published notice for its date of publication the day it appears, and it is a poor use of the remaining days to assume that money produced on the morning of the auction will be accepted as of right.

## Which loans the Act is not allowed to touch

Section 31 puts several categories outside the Act entirely, and three of them account for most of the arguments that succeed at the threshold. Clause (i) excludes any security interest created in agricultural land. Clause (h) excludes a security interest securing repayment of a financial asset not exceeding one lakh rupees. Clause (j) excludes any case in which the amount due is less than twenty per cent of the principal amount and interest thereon.

The agricultural land exclusion is the one most often raised and least often documented. Whether a particular parcel is agricultural land is decided on what the revenue record shows and what the land is in fact used for, not on what the loan documents call it — which is why the jamabandi and the khasra entries are worth obtaining at the outset. Where the security is Rajasthan agricultural land, the position in the revenue record is set out in the note on land revenue laws and the revenue courts, and any conversion of the land's use under Section 90A of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956 is part of the same enquiry.

If Section 31 does take the loan out of the Act, the next question is where the bank must then go, and the Tribunal is not the automatic answer. Section 34 bars the civil court only in respect of a matter which the Debts Recovery Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal "is empowered by or under this Act to determine". The bar therefore reaches exactly as far as the Tribunal's own jurisdiction, and no further. That jurisdiction comes from Section 17(1) of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993: the power to entertain and decide applications from banks and financial institutions for recovery of debts due to them. Section 1(4) of the same Act then withdraws it below a floor. Save as otherwise provided, its provisions do not apply where the amount of debt due is less than ten lakh rupees, or such other amount, being not less than one lakh rupees, as the Central Government may by notification specify. That last clause matters. The operative figure is whatever stands notified on the day, so the notification in force is to be checked and never assumed from the bare section. Below the floor there is no Tribunal to apply to at all: the bank's remedy is an ordinary civil suit in the court of competent pecuniary jurisdiction, with the ordinary defences and the ordinary right of appeal, and Section 34 has nothing to bar. Section 17(1A)(b) of the 1993 Act separately provides for circuit sittings of the Tribunal at all district headquarters, which is a different question from where the Tribunal is permanently established. Which of these routes a particular recovery actually takes is the first thing worth settling, and it is set out beside the other forums in the note on which forum a recovery matter goes to at Jodhpur.

## What should be done in the first week

Take the date of the notice and count sixty days forward on a calendar, in writing. Obtain the statement of account for the whole period of the loan and check the figure demanded against it, item by item, including charges and interest reversals. Obtain the title documents and the revenue record for the mortgaged property and confirm what the property actually is. Then put the objection under Section 13(3A) on record within the sixty days, by a mode that produces proof of delivery, and diarise the fifteenth day after it for the bank's reasons.

If possession is taken, the date it was taken becomes the only date that matters; the application under Section 17 is to be filed within forty-five days of it. A note on the same subject in Hindi, written around the Rajasthan borrower and the Debts Recovery Tribunal as it is encountered here, is available at SARFAESI नोटिस धारा 13(2): बैंक कब्ज़ा और DRT में बचाव.

The later stages each have a page of their own: possession taken through the District Magistrate under Section 14, the application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 17, stopping the auction under Section 13(8), and the appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under Section 18.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a Section 13(2) notice give?
Sixty days from the date of the notice. Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 requires the secured creditor to call upon the borrower, by notice in writing, to discharge in full his liabilities within sixty days, failing which the creditor becomes entitled to exercise the measures in Section 13(4). The account must already stand classified as a non-performing asset.

Can a borrower reply to a Section 13(2) notice, and must the bank answer?
Yes. Under Section 13(3A), if the borrower makes a representation or raises an objection on receipt of the notice, the secured creditor must consider it, and if it is not accepted, must communicate the reasons for non-acceptance to the borrower within fifteen days. The proviso makes clear that the communication of those reasons does not by itself entitle the borrower to apply to the Debts Recovery Tribunal at that stage.

When can a borrower approach the Debts Recovery Tribunal, and within what time?
Once the secured creditor has taken one of the measures in Section 13(4) — most commonly possession of the secured asset. An application under Section 17(1) must then be made to the Debts Recovery Tribunal within forty-five days from the date on which the measure was taken. Under Section 17(1A) it is filed where the cause of action arises, where the secured asset is located, or where the branch maintaining the account is situated.

What has to be deposited to appeal a DRT order to the Appellate Tribunal?
An appeal under Section 18 lies to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal within thirty days of receipt of the DRT's order, and is not entertained unless the borrower deposits fifty per cent of the amount of debt due as claimed by the secured creditor or determined by the Tribunal, whichever is less. The Appellate Tribunal may, for reasons recorded in writing, reduce that amount to not less than twenty-five per cent.

Is agricultural land within the reach of the SARFAESI Act?
No. Section 31(i) states that the provisions of the Act do not apply to any security interest created in agricultural land. Section 31(h) similarly excludes a security interest securing repayment of a financial asset not exceeding one lakh rupees, and Section 31(j) excludes any case in which the amount due is less than twenty per cent of the principal amount and interest thereon.

This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. The steps available to a borrower depend on the terms of the security documents, the conduct of the account, the measure the secured creditor has actually taken and the date on which it was taken. For guidance on a particular matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

# Tenant Eviction in Rajasthan: Grounds and Rent Tribunal Procedure
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/tenant-eviction-rajasthan-rent-control-act.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Tenant Eviction in Rajasthan: Grounds and Procedure Under the Rent Control Act, 2001

Property Law

# Tenant Eviction in Rajasthan: Grounds and Procedure Under the Rent Control Act, 2001

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 June 2026

Landlord–tenant disputes in Rajasthan's cities are governed primarily by the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001, which replaced the old Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act of 1950 and created a specialised forum — the Rent Tribunal — for eviction and rent disputes in the areas to which the Act applies. For premises outside the Act's coverage, the ordinary civil law route under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 remains available. Knowing which regime applies, and what each demands, is the first step in any eviction or tenancy defence strategy.

The statutory grounds for eviction: Under the 2001 Act, a landlord may seek eviction only on the grounds enumerated in the statute. The principal grounds are: (1) default in payment of rent — the tenant has neither paid nor tendered rent for the prescribed period despite the obligation; (2) sub-letting or parting with possession of the premises, in whole or part, without the landlord's written consent; (3) material alteration or damage — the tenant has caused substantial damage to the premises or made structural alterations without consent; (4) change of user — using residential premises for incompatible commercial or other purposes; (5) nuisance to neighbours or the landlord; (6) reasonable and bona fide personal necessity of the landlord or the landlord's family — the most heavily litigated ground; (7) the premises being required for repairs, rebuilding or demolition that cannot be carried out with the tenant in occupation; and (8) the tenant having acquired or built suitable alternative accommodation. Each ground has its own evidentiary requirements, and pleading them precisely matters — eviction petitions fail more often on sloppy pleadings than on weak facts.

Relief against eviction for first default: The Act tempers the default ground with a one-time protection: where the tenant, on the first petition for default, deposits the entire arrears of rent together with interest and the landlord's costs within the time fixed by the Tribunal, eviction on the ground of default is declined. This indulgence is designed for the honest tenant who has fallen behind — it is not available for chronic defaulters, and a second default forfeits the protection. For tenants, the practical rule is simple: deposit first, contest after. Continuing to withhold rent during litigation is the fastest way to lose an otherwise defensible case.

Bona fide personal necessity — how courts test it: The landlord must show that the need is genuine, present and reasonable — not a mere desire or a pretext for extracting higher rent. The settled jurisprudence holds that the landlord is the best judge of their own requirement: courts do not dictate that the landlord should adjust in other premises if the claimed need is honest. Comparative hardship is weighed — what the tenant loses by eviction against what the landlord suffers without the premises — and the availability of alternative accommodation on both sides is a central fact. Tenants defending a personal-necessity petition should investigate and plead the landlord's other properties specifically; landlords should anticipate that line of attack and explain each property's unsuitability in the petition itself.

Procedure before the Rent Tribunal: Eviction petitions under the Act are filed before the Rent Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction, not the civil court. The Tribunal follows a comparatively summary procedure designed to be faster than a regular civil suit: written statement, affidavit evidence with cross-examination where required, and arguments. Appeals lie to the Appellate Rent Tribunal within the statutory limitation, and the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution remains available against jurisdictional errors. The Act also makes provision for expedited recovery of possession for certain categories of landlords — including senior citizens and widows — whose petitions are dealt with on a priority footing.

Premises outside the Act — the Transfer of Property Act route: Where the 2001 Act does not apply to the premises or the tenancy, the landlord proceeds by terminating the tenancy with a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — fifteen days' notice for month-to-month tenancies, expiring with the end of the tenancy month — followed by a civil suit for possession and mesne profits. The Supreme Court has repeatedly clarified that hyper-technical objections to Section 106 notices are disfavoured; what matters is that the intention to terminate is clear. In these suits the tenant cannot claim the statutory protections of the Rent Control Act, and the litigation usually turns on the validity of the notice and proof of the landlord–tenant relationship.

Practical guidance for landlords: Put every tenancy in writing, record the rent and purpose of letting precisely, insist on bank-transfer rent (a clean default record wins cases), and act on defaults promptly rather than letting arrears accumulate for years. Before filing, assemble the title documents, rent record and — for personal necessity — a concrete, documented account of the need. For tenants: pay or tender rent demonstrably even during disputes (money orders and Tribunal deposits leave a paper trail), never sub-let without written consent, and seek advice immediately on receiving a demand notice or petition — the early procedural steps, especially the first-default deposit, often decide the outcome.

Before any of this is drafted it is worth settling where the matter belongs — the Rent Tribunal, the civil court or the High Court — which a separate note on the Jodhpur courts works through.
 
This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal guidance on your matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

# Section 482 BNSS: Anticipatory Bail, Text, Grounds & Procedure
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/anticipatory-bail-bnss.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Section 482 BNSS — Anticipatory Bail: Provision, Grounds & Procedure

Criminal Law

# Section 482 BNSS — Anticipatory Bail: Provision, Grounds & Procedure

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 April 2026

In short: Section 482 of the BNSS, 2023 is the anticipatory bail provision — the successor to Section 438 CrPC. It allows a person who apprehends arrest on an accusation of a non-bailable offence to apply to the Court of Session or the High Court for a direction that, in the event of arrest, he shall be released on bail. Sub-section (2) sets out the conditions a court may attach; sub-section (3) covers arrest without warrant; and sub-section (4) bars anticipatory bail altogether for offences under Sections 65 and 70(2) of the BNS.

Chamber page: anticipatory and regular bail matters at Jodhpur, the Sessions Court and the High Court.

Anticipatory bail is a direction given in advance: if this person is arrested on this accusation, release him on bail. Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 carries that power. It replaced Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 on 1 July 2024. The Court of Session and the High Court hold the power concurrently. At Jodhpur almost every application goes to the Sessions Judge first, and reaches the Rajasthan High Court only if it fails there or if the case has a reason to start higher.

Text of Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

Bare Act, Act No. 46 of 2023 — reproduced verbatim. Replaces Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

(1)When any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section; and that Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail.

(2)When the High Court or the Court of Session makes a direction under sub-section (1), it may include such conditions in such directions in the light of the facts of the particular case, as it may think fit, including— (i) a condition that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required; (ii) a condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer; (iii) a condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court; (iv) such other condition as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of section 480, as if the bail were granted under that section.

(3)If such person is thereafter arrested without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station on such accusation, and is prepared either at the time of arrest or at any time while in the custody of such officer to give bail, he shall be released on bail; and if a Magistrate taking cognizance of such offence decides that a warrant should be issued in the first instance against that person, he shall issue a bailable warrant in conformity with the direction of the Court under sub-section (1).

(4)Nothing in this section shall apply to any case involving the arrest of any person on accusation of having committed an offence under section 65 and sub-section (2) of section 70 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

Sub-section (4) refers to Sections 65 and 70(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — the offences of rape of a woman under sixteen years and gang rape of a woman under eighteen years.  ·  यह धारा हिंदी में पढ़ें →

## What changed from Section 438 CrPC, and what did not
 
Read the two sections side by side and sub-sections (1), (2) and (3) are the same words. The cross-reference in clause (iv) of sub-section (2) moved from Section 437(3) CrPC to Section 480(3) BNSS, which is the matching provision on mandatory bail conditions. The real change is in sub-section (4). Section 438(4) CrPC listed Sections 376(3), 376AB, 376DA and 376DB of the Indian Penal Code. Section 482(4) BNSS lists Section 65 and Section 70(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which are the same offences renumbered: rape of a woman under sixteen, rape of a woman under twelve, and gang rape of a woman under eighteen.
 
So the test, the forum and the conditions are what they were in 1973. What changed around the section matters more. Section 35 BNSS now limits arrest itself, and Section 173(3) BNSS allows a preliminary enquiry before an FIR in a band of offences. Both are discussed below, because they decide whether an application is needed at all.

## Who can apply, and when
 
The words are "reason to believe that he may be arrested". Three points follow from them.
 
First, no FIR is needed. In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980) a Constitution Bench held that registration of a case is not a condition precedent; what is needed is a belief founded on reasonable grounds, not a vague fear. A written complaint to the police, a notice to appear, or a threat of a complaint with the facts spelt out is enough to move. A bare "they may do something" is not.
 
Second, the offence must be non-bailable. For a bailable offence Section 478 BNSS gives bail as of right at the police station, so Section 482 has no work to do.
 
Third, arrest must be a real prospect. Section 35(1)(b) BNSS says that for an offence punishable up to seven years the police may arrest without warrant only if arrest is necessary for one of five listed reasons, and the officer must record those reasons in writing. Where arrest is not required, Section 35(3) obliges the officer to issue a notice to appear instead, and Section 35(5) says a person who complies with that notice shall not be arrested for that offence unless the officer records reasons why he ought to be. Section 35(7) adds that a person above sixty years or infirm, accused of an offence punishable with less than three years, cannot be arrested without prior permission of an officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police. A person holding a Section 35(3) notice and attending on it is often safer than he thinks. The court will ask why he needs more.
 
There is one more clock. Section 173(3) BNSS lets the officer in charge, with permission of a Deputy Superintendent of Police, hold a preliminary enquiry for up to fourteen days before registering a case for a cognizable offence punishable with three years or more but less than seven. During those fourteen days there is no FIR yet, and an application founded on the complaint alone is possible if the facts are concrete.

## Sessions Court or High Court at Jodhpur
 
Both courts have the power. Neither sub-section says which comes first. Practice at the Rajasthan High Court is settled: the Sessions Court is approached first, and the High Court on refusal or where the case has a reason to start there, such as a question the Sessions Judge cannot conveniently decide, or an accused who is a resident of another State and faces several cases. A direct application at the High Court is not barred, but the Bench will ask why the Sessions Court was bypassed, and the answer must be on the record.
 
At the principal seat at Jodhpur the application is registered as an S.B. Criminal Miscellaneous Bail Application under Section 482 BNSS. It is heard by a Single Bench. If arrest is imminent an urgent listing is sought, and the court commonly grants interim protection with a direction to join the investigation and lists the matter after the State files a reply with the case diary.
 
The order of forums also decides the papers. In the Sessions Court the application is filed with the FIR, the applicant's affidavit of facts and antecedents, and a copy of any notice received. At the High Court the refusal order of the Sessions Judge is added, and the grounds answer that order paragraph by paragraph.

## What the court weighs
 
Section 482 does not list factors. The factors come from Sibbia and from thirty years of practice after it: the nature and gravity of the accusation; the applicant's antecedents, including whether he has earlier been in custody on conviction; the possibility of his fleeing; and whether the accusation is made with the object of injuring or humiliating him by having him arrested. Two further points carry weight at Jodhpur in practice. The first is parity: a co-accused on the same footing who already has bail. The second is the stage of investigation: once the charge-sheet is filed without arrest, the need for custodial interrogation has usually gone, and the court says so.
 
The court also asks what custodial interrogation would add. Where the evidence is documentary, a bank record or a registered deed, the answer is usually nothing, and that is a strong ground. Where the recovery of a weapon or of money is pending, the State presses for custody and the application is harder.

## Conditions, bond and sureties
 
Section 482(2) lists three conditions by name: availability for interrogation, no inducement or threat to any person acquainted with the facts, and no leaving India without permission. Clause (iv) imports Section 480(3), which applies where the offence is punishable with seven years or more or falls under Chapter VI, VII or XVII of the BNS, and requires three further terms: attendance under the bond, no similar offence, and no tampering with evidence. In practice the order reads like a standard set: report to the investigating officer on fixed dates, surrender the passport where flight is a live concern, do not contact the complainant.
 
The bond is governed by Section 484 BNSS: its amount is fixed with regard to the circumstances of the case and shall not be excessive, and the High Court or Court of Session may reduce a bail amount demanded by a police officer or Magistrate. Section 485 requires the bond and the sureties' bonds to carry the conditions. Section 486 requires every surety to declare before the court how many persons he already stands surety for. A surety who hides an earlier bond risks the bail itself.
 
Breach of a condition is a ground for cancellation. Section 483(3) BNSS allows the High Court or Court of Session to direct that any person released on bail under Chapter XXXV be arrested and committed to custody. The protection is real, but it is conditional in both directions.

## After the order
 
Sub-section (3) does two things. If the police arrest the person without warrant on that accusation and he is prepared to give bail, the officer in charge shall release him on bail; the direction binds the station. And if a Magistrate taking cognizance decides to issue a warrant in the first instance, it shall be a bailable warrant in conformity with the direction. The order therefore travels with the case into the trial court.
 
Does it lapse when the charge-sheet is filed? No. In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020) a Constitution Bench held that anticipatory bail need not be limited to a fixed period and does not end automatically on the filing of the charge-sheet or on summons; unless the granting court writes in a time limit, the protection continues until the end of the trial. A well-drafted order asks for exactly that.
 
If anticipatory bail is refused and the person is arrested, the remedy moves to regular bail under Section 480 before the Magistrate or under Section 483 before the Sessions Court or High Court. The arithmetic of custody then matters: Section 187(3) BNSS gives default bail after sixty days in custody for most offences and ninety days where the offence is punishable with death, life or ten years or more, if the charge-sheet is not filed by then.

## Where Section 482 does not reach
 
The statutory bar in sub-section (4). No anticipatory bail for an accusation under Section 65 BNS (rape of a woman under sixteen, or under twelve) or Section 70(2) BNS (gang rape of a woman under eighteen). For regular bail in those cases Section 483(1) adds a second proviso: notice of the application to the Public Prosecutor within fifteen days of receipt of the notice, and Section 483(2) makes the presence of the informant or a person authorised by him obligatory at the hearing.
 
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Section 18 says nothing in Section 438 of the Code applies to an accusation under that Act, and Section 18A(2), inserted in 2018, repeats the bar "notwithstanding any judgment or order or direction of any Court". Courts have examined whether the FIR discloses an offence under the Act at all, and where it does not the bar does not operate; where it does, no Section 482 application lies. The remedy against a Special Court order granting or refusing bail is an appeal to the High Court under Section 14A(2) of that Act, to be filed within ninety days under Section 14A(3), with an outer limit of one hundred and eighty days. That appeal, not a fresh bail application, is the route at Jodhpur.
 
NDPS Act, 1985. Section 37(1)(b) bars release on bail for offences under Sections 19, 24 and 27A and for offences involving commercial quantity unless the Public Prosecutor has been heard and the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty and is not likely to offend while on bail. The section does not name anticipatory bail, but these twin conditions apply to it, and for a commercial quantity pre-arrest relief is rarely granted.
 
Economic offences. Section 482 applies, but Section 45 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act carries its own twin conditions and the Enforcement Directorate is a separate arresting agency, so a PMLA accusation is worked separately from the predicate offence.

## Papers to gather before the first hearing

The FIR, if registered. Section 173(2) BNSS gives the informant a free copy; the accused obtains it from the court record or the police website.
 
Any notice under Section 35(3) BNSS, with proof of the dates on which the applicant attended.
 
The complaint or the papers that found the apprehension, where there is no FIR yet.
 
Proof of residence and identity, and of the applicant's roots in the district: employment, property, family.
 
A list of earlier cases, if any, with their stage. Hiding an antecedent is the fastest way to lose the application.
 
Documents that answer the accusation: the agreement, the bank statement, the registered deed, the medical record. These are annexed, not argued from memory.
 
The Sessions Court's refusal order, when the application is at the High Court.

## Step by step at Jodhpur

Fix the offence and its punishment. If it is bailable, Section 478 applies and no application is needed. If it is in Section 482(4), the SC/ST Act or Section 37 NDPS, the route is different, as above.
 
Check Section 35. If a notice to appear has been issued, comply with it and keep the record. The application is stronger with that record and may be unnecessary.
 
Decide the forum: Sessions Court of the district where the case is registered, or the High Court with a reason on record.
 
Draft the grounds around the facts: how the apprehension arose, why custodial interrogation adds nothing, the applicant's roots, parity if any.
 
Seek interim protection on the first date with an undertaking to join the investigation.
 
On the final order, execute the bond and the sureties' bonds with the conditions written in, and serve a copy on the investigating officer and the police station.
 
Keep every condition. Attendance dates and passport surrender are checked when the State moves for cancellation.

How these applications are actually moved, how urgency is sought and what a family should gather before the first hearing is set out in our guide to bail matters in the Jodhpur courts. The five kinds of bail under the BNSS, with default bail and the Section 479 half-sentence rule, are compared in Hindi at ज़मानत के प्रकार और प्रक्रिया.
 
Which court at Jodhpur takes which kind of matter, and what papers to carry to a first meeting, is set out on the page on advocates in Jodhpur and the forums there.

Questions people ask before filing

Can I apply for anticipatory bail before an FIR is registered?
Yes. Section 482(1) BNSS speaks of reason to believe that one may be arrested, not of an FIR. In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980) the Supreme Court held that registration of a case is not a condition precedent, provided the apprehension rests on concrete facts. A complaint to the police, a Section 35(3) notice or a preliminary enquiry under Section 173(3) is enough to found an application if the accusation feared is spelt out.

Should the application be filed in the Sessions Court or directly in the High Court?
Both courts have concurrent power under Section 482 BNSS. At Jodhpur the settled practice is the Sessions Court first and the Rajasthan High Court on refusal, or where a reason to start higher is on record. A direct application is not barred, but the Bench asks why the Sessions Court was bypassed.

Does anticipatory bail end when the charge-sheet is filed?
No. In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020) a Constitution Bench held that the protection need not be limited in time and does not lapse on the filing of the charge-sheet or on summons. Unless the granting court writes in a time limit, it continues until the end of the trial, and Section 482(3) BNSS requires a Magistrate issuing a warrant in the first instance to make it bailable.

Is anticipatory bail available in SC/ST Act or NDPS cases?
Section 18 and Section 18A(2) of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act bar it where the FIR discloses an offence under that Act; the remedy against a Special Court order on bail is an appeal under Section 14A(2) within ninety days. In NDPS matters Section 37(1)(b) applies its twin conditions to offences under Sections 19, 24, 27A and to commercial quantity, so pre-arrest relief is rarely granted there.

What conditions does the court usually impose?
Section 482(2) BNSS names three: availability for interrogation, no inducement or threat to witnesses, and no leaving India without permission. Clause (iv) imports the Section 480(3) conditions for offences punishable with seven years or more. Courts commonly add passport surrender and fixed reporting dates. Breach allows cancellation under Section 483(3).

Which offences are excluded by Section 482(4) BNSS?
Accusations under Section 65 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (rape of a woman under sixteen years, and under twelve years) and Section 70(2) (gang rape of a woman under eighteen years). In those cases only regular bail can be sought, with notice to the Public Prosecutor under the second proviso to Section 483(1) and the informant's presence under Section 483(2).

This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal guidance on your matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

Shubham Ojha & Associates
 
Advocates, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur  ·  +91 70230 51275  ·  WhatsApp

# Power of Attorney from Abroad for Property in India
URL: https://shubhamojhaandassociates.com/articles/power-of-attorney-from-abroad-property-india.html

Home
 ›
 Legal Insights
 ›
 Power of Attorney from Abroad

Property Law

# I live abroad and must give a power of attorney for property in India. What must it say, and what can it not do?

By Shubham Ojha, BA LL.B., LL.M., ICWA (Foundation) | Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur
 
 August 2026

A power of attorney executed outside India is recognised for registration only where it has been executed before, and authenticated by, a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government — Section 33(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908. It may then be stamped in India within three months after it is first received here.

At a glance

Who may authenticate it, if you do not reside in India — a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government. These alone are recognised (Section 33(1)(c), Registration Act, 1908)
 
What that recognition is for — it lets your agent present the document for registration on your behalf (Section 32(c), Registration Act, 1908)
 
Time to stamp it in India — three months after it is first received in India, not three months from signature abroad (Section 18(1), Indian Stamp Act, 1899); where a private person cannot duly stamp it, it goes to the Collector within the same three months (Section 18(2))
 
What the attorney may sign — the donee may execute an instrument in his own name and signature, by the donor's authority, and it is as effectual in law as if the donor had signed it (Section 2, Powers-of-Attorney Act, 1882)
 
Proof in court — a power of attorney authenticated by those officers is presumed to have been so executed and authenticated (Section 84, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023)
 
What it can never do — transfer ownership. "A SA/GPA/WILL transaction does not convey any title nor create any interest in an immovable property"; property passes "only by a registered deed of conveyance" (Suraj Lamp & Industries (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Supreme Court, 11 October 2011)

Jurisdiction. The Registration Act, 1908, the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, the Powers-of-Attorney Act, 1882 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 are central statutes and apply across India. Rates of stamp duty, and some of the procedure at the registering office, are dealt with by the State concerned, so the duty payable and the local practice must be confirmed for the district where the property lies. Where this note refers to the jamabandi and to mutation, that material is specific to Rajasthan. Consultation by telephone and video is available for clients residing outside India; Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961 entitles an advocate to practise throughout India.

## Who can authenticate it where you are?

This is the question to settle before anything is drafted, because getting it wrong is not a drafting error that can be corrected later — the document simply will not be accepted, and by the time that is discovered the signatory is usually back in another country.

Section 33(1) of the Registration Act, 1908 is unusually blunt about it. For the purposes of Section 32, it says, "the following powers-of-attorney shall alone be recognized". Clause (c) governs the person living overseas: if the principal, at the time of executing the power of attorney, does not reside in India, what is recognised is a power of attorney "executed before and authenticated by a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government".

Two words in that clause do most of the work, and both are routinely missed. The first is "before". The instrument must be executed before the authenticating officer — signed in his presence, not signed at home on Sunday and carried to him on Monday for a stamp. The second is "alone". A power of attorney witnessed by two colleagues, or sworn before an employer, or attested at a bank, is not within the clause however genuine it is.

Section 32 explains what the recognition is for. Every document to be registered must be presented at the proper registration office by the person executing or claiming under it, by his representative or assign, or — clause (c) — "by the agent of such person, representative or assign, duly authorised by power-of-attorney executed and authenticated in manner hereinafter mentioned". Sections 32 and 33 are therefore one mechanism read in two halves: 32 says who may walk into the Sub-Registrar's office with the deed, and 33 says which power of attorney entitles him to.

The clause offers a choice, and in practice the choice matters. Authentication at the Indian Mission — Embassy, High Commission or Consulate — takes longer and costs the client a working day, but it is the route no registering office has ever queried in front of me. A foreign Notary Public is squarely within the clause, and is usually far quicker; whether the office where the property lies will also want the notarial act legalised or apostilled before it accepts the document is a matter of local practice rather than of the section, and it is worth one telephone call to the Sub-Registrar concerned before the client signs, not after. I have had to send a client in Sharjah back to a notary twice for want of that call.

## General or special: which one should actually be executed?

Almost every person who writes to me from abroad asks for a general power of attorney, and in most matters a general power is the wrong instrument.

A general power authorises the holder to do a class of things — to manage, to let, to appear, to sell, sometimes all of them — in respect of everything the donor owns. A special power authorises named acts in respect of a named property. The convenience of the general power is real: one document, executed once, covers whatever comes up. That convenience is also exactly the risk, because the holder's authority does not lapse when the relationship does.

A fair share of the property disputes that reach the Jodhpur Bench from families with a member overseas began with a general power given years earlier, in good faith, to the brother who was already looking after the land. Nobody withdrew it, because nobody remembered it existed. What is done under it while it subsists is done with the donor's authority, and the person on the other side of the transaction — the buyer, the bank — is entitled to look at the instrument and act on it.

So the working rule I give is a narrow one. Execute a special power, confined to the specific property, described by khasra or plot number and by the record in which it stands; state the specific acts authorised; where a sale or a mortgage is contemplated, say so in terms rather than relying on a general clause; and give it an end date. A power of attorney with an expiry is a much smaller thing to have forgotten about than one without.

## What must the document actually contain?

Section 2 of the Powers-of-Attorney Act, 1882 sets the reason why the wording carries so much weight. The donee, it provides, "may, if he thinks fit, execute or do any instrument or thing in and with his own name and signature, and his own seal, where sealing is required, by the authority of the donor of the power; and every instrument and thing so executed and done, shall be as effectual in law as if it had been executed or done by the donee of the power in the name, and with the signature and seal, of the donor thereof."

Read that carefully and the whole drafting discipline follows from four words: by the authority of the donor. The agent's signature binds the principal exactly so far as authority was given, and no further. Everything the instrument does not say, the agent cannot do. A deed signed outside the authority is not cured by the fact that the power of attorney was properly authenticated abroad.

In practical terms the document needs the donor and the donee identified in full and consistently with their identity documents; the property identified by its record particulars, not by a description such as "my ancestral house"; each act authorised set out separately; an express statement of whether the donee may receive sale consideration, and into which account; a clear duration; and the manner of revocation. Where the donor is a non-resident, the document should also record the passport particulars used at the place of authentication, since that is the identity the authenticating officer certifies.

One further point that is invisible until it is tested. Section 84 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 provides that the Court "shall presume that every document purporting to be a power-of-attorney, and to have been executed before, and authenticated by, a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government, was so executed and authenticated." That presumption is worth a great deal in a contested suit, because it spares the donor the task of proving from abroad that he signed. It attaches to the mode of authentication, not to the elegance of the drafting — which is why the choice made in the first section of this note governs everything that comes after it.

## How long is there to stamp it once it reaches India?

Section 18(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 gives the period, and its wording repays attention: every instrument chargeable with duty "executed only out of India", other than a bill of exchange or a promissory note, "may be stamped within three months after it has been first received in India".

The three months run from first receipt in India — not from the date of signature abroad, and not from the date the agent decides to use it. A power of attorney signed in Toronto in March and couriered to Jodhpur in September is in time if it is stamped by December. This is a genuinely useful provision for families who execute the document during a visit home and then send it on months later, and it is the one that is most often assumed to run the other way.

Section 18(2) covers the case where the instrument cannot, given the description of stamp prescribed for it, be duly stamped by a private person. It may then be taken to the Collector within the same period of three months, and the Collector shall stamp it in the manner the State Government prescribes. The subsection is a route, not an extension: the three months are the same three months. What the duty comes to is fixed by the State schedule applicable where the instrument is used, and must be ascertained for that State — it is not a figure that can be assumed from another State's practice.

## What a power of attorney cannot do

It cannot transfer ownership. Not a well-drafted one, not a registered one, not one that recites that consideration has passed.

In Suraj Lamp & Industries (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, decided by the Supreme Court on 11 October 2011, the Court addressed the practice of transferring property by a bundle of a sale agreement, a general power of attorney and a will. Its conclusion was stated without qualification: "a SA/GPA/WILL transaction does not convey any title nor create any interest in an immovable property", and immovable property "can be legally and lawfully transferred/conveyed only by a registered deed of conveyance".

The consequences of that holding are still arriving in chambers fifteen years later, and they arrive most painfully in matters with a non-resident in them. A person abroad is told that the land has been "given" to a relative or a purchaser by power of attorney and that nothing further is needed. It has not been given. Whatever was intended, title has not moved, and the reckoning tends to come at the next mutation, the next sale, or the next death in either family — by which time the witnesses to what was actually agreed are frequently gone.

It is equally important to state what the judgment did not do, because it is often quoted too widely. The Court said in terms that its observations "are not intended to in any way affect the validity of sale agreements and powers of attorney executed in genuine transactions", giving as an example a power given "to his spouse, son, daughter, brother, sister or a relative to manage his affairs". A genuine power of attorney remains a perfectly good instrument for its proper purpose — to authorise someone to act. What it is not is a substitute for the conveyance.

The related question of whether the power of attorney must itself be registered turns on a different provision. Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 makes registration compulsory for non-testamentary instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest in immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards. An instrument that merely authorises an agent to act does not on its face do any of those things; its use at the registering office is governed instead by Sections 32 and 33. Because States have made their own requirements in this area, the position for the district where the property lies should be confirmed before the document is executed abroad rather than after it lands. If the office refuses, the next step is not a suit. Section 72 of the Registration Act gives an appeal to the Registrar to whom that Sub-Registrar is subordinate, to be presented within thirty days, unless the refusal rests on a denial of execution, in which case Section 73 applies instead. A quarrel about the instrument itself goes elsewhere again: cancellation is a civil suit under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and Section 31(2) obliges the court to send its decree to the office where the document was registered so that the cancellation is noted on the record, whereas a mutation entered on the strength of a power is undone in the revenue court and not the civil one. Which of those doors a matter here opens at is set out in the note on the chamber at Jodhpur and the forums it appears before.

## What should be done first, from where you are?

Three steps, in this order.

Read the record before drafting the authority. The jamabandi or record of rights and the mutation entries tell you whose name the property actually stands in today, and it is not always the name the family assumes. A power of attorney drawn for the wrong recorded holder is waste paper, and the fact is far cheaper to establish before a client takes a day off work to attend a Consulate. Where the property was inherited, the sequence is set out in the note on securing inherited land in Rajasthan from abroad.

Settle the mode of authentication with the office that will receive the document. Consulate or notary, and if notary then whether legalisation is also expected in that district. This is a single enquiry and it removes the only failure that cannot be repaired remotely.

Choose the holder on the assumption that the relationship may not last. This is the least legal and most useful part of the advice. The instrument should be narrow enough that it is safe in the hands of someone you may one day disagree with, and it should be dated to expire. Where a relative is already in occupation, the position is different again and is dealt with in the note on recovering possession from a relative; and where several heirs hold together, the shares are better settled between them, by partition or family settlement, before any authority to deal with the property is given to one of them.

This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. The form of authority required, the stamp duty payable and the practice of the registering office differ with the State, the property and the transaction proposed. For guidance on a particular matter, please consult a qualified advocate.

Shubham Ojha & Associates
 
Advocate, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur  ·  Enrolment No. R/2958/2020 (Bar Council of Rajasthan)  ·  +91 70230 51275  ·  WhatsApp
